lesson.title: Where to Push: Finding the Weak Points in a Strong System
lesson.summary: Systems thinking's idea of leverage points, places where a small, well chosen intervention produces a large system wide change, offers a practical way to interrupt a self sustaining hype cycle rather than trying to fight it everywhere at once.
lesson.body:
The leverage points concept, drawn from systems thinking, ranks the places you can intervene in a system from weak to strong. Low leverage points are things like adjusting a single number or parameter, which usually get absorbed by the rest of the system with little lasting effect. High leverage points are things like changing the system's underlying goals, the information it has access to, or the rules that structure who benefits from what, changes that can reshape the system's whole trajectory rather than nudging one variable at a time.

Applied to the self sustaining hype cycle from the previous chapter, this hierarchy explains why some well intentioned corrections barely matter while others could actually work. Fact checking a single press release, or publishing one skeptical paper questioning an overhyped claim, is a low leverage move: the hype reinforcement loop, the sunk cost escalation loop, the geopolitical arms race loop, and the career incentive loop all keep running through their own separate channels regardless of that one correction. Higher leverage interventions target the structure itself: changing funding rules so that grant renewal depends partly on independently verified progress rather than self reported milestones, requiring public disclosure of realistic error bars and timelines rather than point estimates, or changing what journals, conference committees, and hiring panels reward, so that calibrated, honest uncertainty is treated as a sign of scientific maturity rather than a career liability.

A concrete illustration makes the distinction sharper. Imagine a funding agency that ties a meaningful fraction of a lab's next grant renewal to how accurate that lab's previous roadmap predictions turned out to be, rather than simply to how much progress the lab claims to have made. That single rule change alters the goal the whole system is optimizing for, which is a high leverage point in Meadows style systems thinking, as opposed to adding one more layer of review, which is a low leverage parameter tweak. It also directly counteracts the professor grant conflicts pressure described back in the career incentive loop chapter, because it makes honest calibration pay rather than punishing it.

None of this is easy, and the most powerful leverage points, changing the deeper goals and mental models a whole research culture organizes around, are also the hardest to move, since they require coordinated change across funders, institutions, and norms rather than any single actor's decision. But individuals are not powerless while waiting for institutions to reform themselves. A prospective student or investor who insists on calibrated, specific information before committing years or dollars is applying a personal leverage point of their own, refusing to let their individual decision simply become one more input that keeps the larger cycle spinning. That personal leverage point is exactly what the chapters on informed consent and ethical investment duty later in this book will make concrete.
